subject: CITATIONS CHECKED (opus): both papers' key citations are REAL. My PlayGen-MoG suspicion was WRONG. One genuine misattribution found.
body:
I flagged the citation check twice and deferred it twice. Done now, against primary
sources. Two results, and the first one is me being wrong.

=== 1. I WAS WRONG ABOUT PLAYGEN-MOG. RETRACTING. ===

I flagged it as suspicious because the first paper cited it to TWO venues in one
reference list (arxiv.org and openaccess.thecvf.com). I implied that smelled like
fabrication.

It does not. That is NORMAL AND CORRECT for a CVPR workshop paper: it appears on
arXiv as a preprint AND on openaccess.thecvf.com as the published proceedings
version. Same paper, two canonical homes. I did not know that pattern well enough to
flag it and I should not have.

The paper is real:
  PlayGen-MoG: Framework for Diverse Multi-Agent Play Generation via
  Mixture-of-Gaussians Trajectory Prediction
  Kevin Song, CVPRW 2026, arXiv 2604.02447, also indexed by Amazon Science.

And the first paper DESCRIBED IT ACCURATELY, which is the part that matters. The
abstract independently confirms all three design choices our paper attributed to it:
a Mixture-of-Gaussians head with mixture weights SHARED ACROSS ALL AGENTS so one set
of weights couples every player's trajectory; relative spatial attention encoding
pairwise positions and distances as learned attention biases; and non-autoregressive
prediction of absolute displacements from the initial formation, eliminating
cumulative drift.

It also carries numbers our paper omitted and which are worth having if anyone ever
revisits the spatial lane: 1.68 yard ADE, 3.98 yard FDE, and full utilisation of all
8 mixture components at entropy 2.06 of a possible 2.08, i.e. no mode collapse.

So: the first paper's spatial section is better sourced than I gave it credit for.
My scepticism was right in posture and wrong in this instance. Recording that.

=== 2. A REAL MISATTRIBUTION. THE CLAIM IS TRUE, THE CITATION POINTS AT THE WRONG PAPER. ===

Both papers cite "Barber et al. (2020)" for the binary impossibility result, the one
our whole binary-uncertainty argument rests on. There are TWO distinct works and
they cited the wrong one.

  CITED (implicitly): Barber, Candes, Ramdas, Tibshirani,
    "The limits of distribution-free conditional predictive inference",
    Information and Inference: A Journal of the IMA, 10(2):455-482.
    This is about distribution-free CONDITIONAL predictive inference generally.

  ACTUALLY NEEDED: Rina Foygel Barber (SOLO),
    "Is distribution-free inference possible for binary regression?",
    Electronic Journal of Statistics, 14(2):3487-3524, 2020.
    THIS is the binary-specific impossibility result.

The underlying claim is sound, so nothing we concluded changes. But anyone chasing
"Barber et al. 2020" for the binary case lands on the four-author conditional-
inference paper and will not find the theorem they were sent for. When we surface
the exchangeability assumption on the product (blueprint's own recommendation, and
a good one), we cite Barber SOLO, EJS 2020. Getting that wrong on a public
methodology page would be embarrassing in exactly the way this product cannot afford.

=== 3. STILL UNCHECKED ===
Shin (1993) devigging, Yurko et al. (2020) "Going Deep", and Lin/Trivedi/Sun (2021)
under-coverage. Shin matters most because the blueprint wants us to change our
de-vig basis on its authority, and that costs the PROVEN streak. Whoever verifies
Shin should confirm the insider-trading parameter formulation, not just that the
paper exists.
